summary: This document registers a new "fax" media feature tag for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP). Without it, a fax call looks just like a voice call when it starts, so it can be routed to a device that cannot handle faxes. With the tag and caller preferences, SIP networks can route fax calls more accurately.

plainLanguage.summary: A fax call and a phone call look the same when they ring. This adds a little label saying "this one is a fax," so it goes to a machine that can actually receive it.

questions: how to indicate fax capability in sip
what is the sip fax feature tag
how to route fax calls in sip
what is sip.fax t38 vs passthrough
how does sip know a call is a fax
subtitle: A SIP feature tag that lets a call say up front that it is a fax, so it reaches a fax-capable device.

tldr.problem: SIP sets fax calls up as voice calls first, so a fax can be routed to a SIP user agent that cannot handle faxes.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the sip.fax media feature tag with values t38 and passthrough. Fax-capable devices register it, and callers ask for it in the Accept-Contact header of an INVITE, using the caller preferences of RFC 3841.
tldr.outcome: Servers that implement RFC 3840 and RFC 3841 can steer fax calls to fax-capable devices. Callers should state a preference rather than a requirement, because a requirement can make the call fail.

today: RFC 6913 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the definition of the sip.fax media feature tag.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Fax over IP in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) is handled in a voice first manner. Nothing in the initial INVITE shows that the caller wants a fax transport protocol such as ITU-T T.38. The call is set up as voice, and only after it connects does a switch to T.38 occur. As a result, fax calls can be routed to SIP user agents (UAs) that are not fax capable.

The RFC proposes using the caller preferences of RFC 3841, which let UAs express preferences that SIP servers take into account. It defines a "fax" media feature tag for the SIP tree, as per Section 12.1 of RFC 3840.
sections.plainLanguage: Fax calls start out pretending to be phone calls, so they can end up at a phone that cannot take a fax. The fix is a label that says fax from the start.

sections.title: Why Not Use SDP?
sections.content:
Normally capabilities are handled in the Session Description Protocol (SDP) part of a SIP exchange. Fax is unusual because the real intention of the call is not accurately signaled in the initial SDP exchange. Indications of T.38 or another fax transport are not known when the INVITE is sent, and fax calls are always treated as voice calls until they connect.

The RFC gives an example. Alice wants to send a fax to Bob, who has registered two UAs, one not fax capable and one supporting T.38. SIP servers cannot tell that Alice prefers a fax-capable UA, and they do not know which of Bob's UAs can do fax. With the new tag, Bob's UAs state their capabilities at registration, Alice states her preference up front, and the call goes to the fax-capable UA.
sections.plainLanguage: The usual note that describes a call does not say it is a fax until too late. Bob has two phones, and only one takes faxes, so a label lets the system pick the right one.

sections.title: Using the sip.fax Tag
sections.content:
sip.fax is a new string parameter. A receiving UA includes it in the Contact header field of REGISTER messages to say it is fax capable, and a SIP Registrar includes it in the Contact header of its 200 OK to confirm, all as per RFC 3840.

A calling UA SHOULD include sip.fax in the Accept-Contact header of an INVITE to ask for routing to a fax-capable UA. Without it, fax call determination is not possible until after the call connects. If the network elements implement the procedures of RFC 3840 and RFC 3841, the call is preferentially routed to UAs that advertised support.

A caller could express a requirement instead of a preference, but the RFC says it SHOULD NOT. The call could fail because no receiving UA advertised support, or because some network element does not support the processing. A caller that does require it should be ready to relax it to a preference if it receives a failure response saying the requirement mechanism is not supported.

The tag has two allowed values. t38 means the call uses ITU-T T.38. passthrough means the ITU-T G.711 codec carries the fax.
sections.plainLanguage: A phone that can take faxes puts the sticker on its registration. A caller who wants to send a fax asks for a phone with that sticker. It is better to ask nicely than to demand, because demanding might mean nobody answers.

sections.title: Registration and INVITE Example
sections.content:
In the RFC's example, Bob's UA sends a REGISTER whose Contact header carries +sip.fax="t38" and an Expires of 3600. The registrar replies with a 200 OK that repeats the tag in its Contact header.

Callers who want fax then include the tag in the Accept-Contact header of their INVITE, as in Accept-Contact: *;+sip.fax="t38".
sections.plainLanguage: Bob's phone tells the office it takes faxes, and the office says okay. Later, Alice's call says it wants a fax phone.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC adds no new security text of its own. It says the security considerations for media feature tags from Section 11.1 of RFC 3840 apply.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing new here. The safety rules for labels like this were already written down in an earlier RFC.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content:
The RFC adds a new media feature tag to the SIP Media Feature Tag Registration Tree, following RFC 2506 and RFC 3840. The tag name is sip.fax and its ASN.1 identifier is 1.3.6.1.8.4.25.

Values are tokens with an equality relationship. t38 means the device supports the image/t38 media type and ITU-T T.38 for carrying T.30 and T.4 fax data over IP. passthrough means the device supports audio/pcmu and audio/pcma for carrying T.30 and T.4 fax data with the G.711 codec, with further recommendations in ITU-T V.152, Sections 6 and 6.1. The registration says the tag is most useful for early identification of a Fax over IP (FoIP) call.
sections.plainLanguage: The sticker was entered in an official list, with its two allowed words and what each means.
